summary.text: The truncated sum is rewritten as a coefficient of \((1+X)^{(m+2)N}\Phi(X)\), up to a constant exceptional term, where \((1+X+X^2)\Phi=1-X^2\); expanding \((1+X)^p=1+X^p+p\Delta_p\) reduces the comparison to correction terms involving powers of \(\Delta_p\). For \(p\ge5\), \(X^2+X+1\) divides \(\Delta_p\) and reciprocity makes \(\Delta_p^{i+1}\Phi\) anti-palindromic, so complementary coefficients pair into falling-factorial differences divisible by \(p^{3(k-1)}\), while the explicit powers of \(p\) and the bound \(v_p(i!)\le i-3\) yield divisibility by \(p^{3k}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}=1+x+2x^2+5x^3+\cdots
\]
be the Catalan generating function. We prove a slightly more general statement, valid for every integer exponent parameter \(m\). The desired result for A333096 is the case \(m=4\).

Throughout, for an integer \(z\) and a nonnegative integer \(r\), write
\[
\binom zr=\frac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-r+1)}{r!}.
\]
This is an integer, including when \(z<0\). We also use
\[
(z)_{\underline r}=z(z-1)\cdots(z-r+1),\qquad (z)_{\underline0}=1.
\]
Thus \(r!\binom zr=(z)_{\underline r}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Rewriting the sequence as one coefficient
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The standard Lagrange-inversion formula for powers of the Catalan series gives, for every integer \(r\),
\[
[x^j]c(x)^r=
\begin{cases}
1,&j=0,\\[2mm]
\displaystyle \binom{r+2j-1}{j}-\binom{r+2j-1}{j-1},&j\ge1.
\end{cases}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
When the displayed quotient is nonsingular, the second line is equivalently
\[
\frac r{r+j}\binom{r+2j-1}{j}.
\]
Indeed, the identity
\[
(j+1)\binom M{j+1}=(M-j)\binom Mj
\]
shows directly that these two expressions agree. Formula (1), being a difference of generalized binomial coefficients, remains meaningful in the exceptional case \(r+j=0\).

Define
\[
T_r(0)=1,
\qquad
T_r(j)=\binom{r+2j-1}{j}-\binom{r+2j-1}{j-1}\quad(j\ge1).
\]
Then the value at \(1\) of the Taylor truncation through degree \(N\) of \(c(x)^{mN}\) is
\[
A_m(N)=\sum_{j=0}^N T_{mN}(j).                                  \tag{2}
\]
In particular, \(a(N)=A_4(N)\) is A333096.

We next encode (2) as a coefficient. For an integer \(M\), let
\[
B_M(X)=\sum_{j\ge0}\binom MjX^j=(1+X)^M
\]
as a formal power series. Define integers
\[
e(0)=1,
\qquad
e(d)=
\begin{cases}
2,&d>0\text{ and }3\mid d,\\
-1,&d>0\text{ and }3\nmid d,
\end{cases}
\]
and put
\[
\Phi(X)=\sum_{d\ge0}e(d)X^d.
\]
The three consecutive positive-index values of \(e\) sum to zero. Checking the first three coefficients separately and thereafter grouping three consecutive terms gives
\[
(1+X+X^2)\Phi(X)=1-X^2.                                        \tag{3}
\]

We claim that, for \(N>0\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^N T_r(j)=[X^N]\bigl(B_{r+2N}(X)\Phi(X)\bigr).        \tag{4}
\]
Here is a direct proof. For \(N=0\), both sides are \(1\). In passing from \(N\) to \(N+1\), use
\[
B_{r+2N+2}=B_{r+2N}(1+X)^2.
\]
By (3),
\[
B_{r+2N}(1+X)^2\Phi
 =B_{r+2N}(1-X^2)+X B_{r+2N}\Phi.
\]
Taking the coefficient of \(X^{N+1}\), the second term supplies the previous coefficient, while the first supplies
\[
\binom{r+2N}{N+1}-\binom{r+2N}{N-1}.
\]
Two applications of Pascal’s identity reduce the increase to
\[
\binom{r+2N+1}{N+1}-\binom{r+2N+1}{N}=T_r(N+1).
\]
This proves (4) by induction.

Applying (4) with \(r=mN\) gives the particularly useful formula
\[
A_m(N)=[X^N]\bigl(B_{(m+2)N}\Phi\bigr).                        \tag{5}
\]

The quotient definition used in the stated generalized sequence agrees with (1) except when \(m=-1\) and \(j=N\): at that point its denominator is zero and its integer-division convention contributes \(0\), whereas the binomial-difference manipulation differs by one. Consequently that normalization satisfies
\[
a_m(N)=[X^N](B_{(m+2)N}\Phi)+\mathbf1_{m=-1}\qquad(N>0).       \tag{6}
\]
The extra term is independent of \(N\), so it cancels in every congruence below. For \(m=4\), no exceptional term occurs and (5) is exactly the OEIS sequence.

It therefore remains to prove the following coefficient theorem. If \(p\ge5\) is prime, \(k\ge1\), \(N>0\), \(p^{k-1}\mid N\), and \(s\in\mathbb Z\), then
\[
[X^{pN}]B_{spN}\Phi-[X^N]B_{sN}\Phi\equiv0\pmod{p^{3k}}.      \tag{7}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The polynomial \(\Delta_p\) and its cubic-root factor
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define the integral polynomial
\[
\Delta_p(X)=\frac{(1+X)^p-1-X^p}{p}
           =\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}\frac1p\binom prX^r.                \tag{8}
\]
Its coefficients are integral because \(p\mid\binom pr\) for \(0<r<p\). Notice that
\[
\deg\Delta_p\le p-1,
\qquad
\Delta_p(0)=0,                                                  \tag{9}
\]
and binomial symmetry gives the reciprocal identity
\[
X^p\Delta_p(X^{-1})=\Delta_p(X).                               \tag{10}
\]
Both the constant and the \(X^p\)-coefficient are zero, so reflection about degree \(p\) is legitimate despite the sharper degree bound in (9).

A key fact is
\[
1+X+X^2\mid\Delta_p(X).                                        \tag{11}
\]
To see this, let \(\zeta\) satisfy \(\zeta^2+\zeta+1=0\). Then \(\zeta^3=1\) and \(1+\zeta=-\zeta^2\). Since \(p\ge5\) is prime, it is odd and not divisible by \(3\). Hence \(p\equiv1\) or \(2\pmod3\), and
\[
(1+\zeta)^p-1-\zeta^p
 =-\zeta^{2p}-1-\zeta^p=0,
\]
because \(\zeta^p\) and \(\zeta^{2p}\) are \(\zeta,\zeta^2\) in one order or the other. Thus \(1+X+X^2\) divides the numerator in (8). Over \(\mathbb Q[X]\), division by the nonzero scalar \(p\) shows that it divides \(\Delta_p\); since the divisor is monic and \(\Delta_p\in\mathbb Z[X]\), the quotient again has integral coefficients. Write
\[
\Delta_p=(1+X+X^2)\Delta'_p.                                   \tag{12}
\]
By (9),
\[
\deg\Delta'_p\le p-3.                                         \tag{13}
\]

For \(i\ge0\), define
\[
P_i(X)=\Delta_p(X)^i\Delta'_p(X)(1-X^2).                       \tag{14}
\]
Equations (3) and (12) imply, as an identity of formal power series,
\[
\Delta_p^{i+1}\Phi=P_i.                                       \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, multiplication of both sides by the nonzero series \(1+X+X^2\) reduces the assertion to
\[
\Delta_p^{i+1}(1-X^2)
 =(1+X+X^2)\Delta_p^i\Delta'_p(1-X^2).
\]
Moreover, (9), (13), and (14) give
\[
\deg P_i\le i(p-1)+(p-3)+2=(i+1)(p-1).                        \tag{16}
\]

We also need an antisymmetry. If reflection about degree \(d\) is denoted by
\[
F^*(X)=X^dF(X^{-1}),
\]
then (10) says that \(\Delta_p\) is symmetric about degree \(p\); \(1+X+X^2\) is symmetric about degree \(2\); and
\[
X^2(1-X^{-2})=-(1-X^2).
\]
Reflecting the identity
\[
(1+X+X^2)P_i=\Delta_p^{i+1}(1-X^2)
\]
about total degree \(2+(i+1)p\), and then cancelling the nonzero polynomial \(1+X+X^2\), yields
\[
X^{(i+1)p}P_i(X^{-1})=-P_i(X).                                 \tag{17}
\]

Set
\[
\pi_i(L)=[X^{pL}]P_i(X)=[X^{pL}](\Delta_p^{i+1}\Phi).          \tag{18}
\]
From (17), whenever \(0\le L\le i+1\),
\[
\pi_i(i+1-L)=-\pi_i(L).                                        \tag{19}
\]
There are two useful endpoint/support facts. First,
\[
\pi_i(0)=0,                                                     \tag{20}
\]
because \(\Delta_p(0)=0\) and the left side of (18) contains \(\Delta_p^{i+1}\). Second, by (16),
\[
\pi_i(L)=0\qquad(L\ge i+1),                                   \tag{21}
\]
since \((i+1)(p-1)<p(i+1)\le pL\). In particular both endpoints in (19) vanish.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. A truncated binomial expansion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Equation (8) is
\[
(1+X)^p=1+X^p+p\Delta_p.                                       \tag{22}
\]
For every integer \(M\), the generalized binomial expansion in the term \(p\Delta_p\), truncated after degree \(r\) in that term, is
\[
B_{pM}(X)\equiv
\sum_{j=0}^{r}\binom Mj(p\Delta_p)^j(1+X^p)^{M-j}
\pmod{X^{r+1}}.                                                 \tag{23}
\]
This is simply
\[
(1+X)^{pM}=\bigl(1+X^p+p\Delta_p\bigr)^M,
\]
expanded around the unit \(1+X^p\). It is valid for negative as well as nonnegative \(M\): the usual recursion
\(B_{M+1}=B_M(1+X)\), together with Pascal’s identity for generalized binomial coefficients, proves it in both integer directions. Since \(X\mid\Delta_p\), every omitted term is divisible by \(X^{r+1}\).

Take \(r=pN\), multiply (23) by \(\Phi\), and extract the coefficient of \(X^{pN}\). In the \(j\)-th term, write
\[
(1+X^p)^{M-j}=B_{M-j}(X^p)=\sum_{l\ge0}\binom{M-j}{l}X^{pl}.
\]
We obtain
\[
[X^{pN}]B_{pM}\Phi
=\sum_{j=0}^{pN}\binom Mj p^j
  \sum_{l=0}^{N}[X^{p(N-l)}](\Delta_p^j\Phi)\binom{M-j}{l}.    \tag{24}
\]
Because \(p\ne3\), multiplication by \(p\) preserves divisibility by \(3\), and therefore
\[
e(pd)=e(d)\qquad(d\ge0).                                     \tag{25}
\]
The \(j=0\) term of (24) is consequently
\[
\sum_{l=0}^N e(p(N-l))\binom Ml
=\sum_{l=0}^N e(N-l)\binom Ml
=[X^N]B_M\Phi.                                                  \tag{26}
\]
Using (18) in all remaining terms and replacing \(j\) by \(i+1\), we get the exact difference formula
\[
\begin{split}
 &[X^{pN}]B_{pM}\Phi-[X^N]B_M\Phi\\
 &\quad=\sum_{i=0}^{pN-1}\binom M{i+1}p^{i+1}
       \sum_{l=0}^{N}\pi_i(N-l)\binom{M-i-1}{l}.               \tag{27}
\end{split}
\]
We will prove that every outer summand is divisible by \(p^{3k}\) when \(M=sN\) and \(p^{k-1}\mid N\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. A falling-factorial divisibility lemma
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For an integer lower index, define
\[
\mathcal C(z,t)=
\begin{cases}
\binom zt,&t\ge0,\\
0,&t<0.
\end{cases}
\]
We first establish an elementary identity. If \(0\le L\le j\), then
\[
\begin{split}
&j!\binom xj\bigl(\mathcal C(x-j,N-L)-
                  \mathcal C(x-j,N-(j-L))\bigr)\\
&\quad=\binom xN\Bigl((x-N)_{\underline{j-L}}N_{\underline L}
                    -(x-N)_{\underline L}N_{\underline{j-L}}\Bigr).   \tag{28}
\end{split}
\]
For example, the first product identity underlying (28) is
\[
j!\binom xj\mathcal C(x-j,N-L)
 =\binom xN (x-N)_{\underline{j-L}}N_{\underline L}.            \tag{29}
\]
If \(L\le N\), multiply both sides by \((N-L)!\) and use
\(r!\binom zr=(z)_{\underline r}\). Both sides then become the same falling factorial \((x)_{\underline{N+j-L}}\), split once after \(j\) factors and once after \(N\) factors, with
\(N!=(N-L)!N_{\underline L}\). If \(L>N\), both sides of (29) are zero, by the definition of \(\mathcal C\) and because \(N_{\underline L}=0\). This proves (29). Replacing \(L\) by \(j-L\) gives the second term of (28).

We also require the following three-factor lemma. Suppose integers \(q,N,u\) satisfy
\[
q\mid N,\qquad q\mid u,\qquad q\mid u-N.                       \tag{30}
\]
Then, for positive integers \(a,b\),
\[
q^3\mid
(u)_{\underline b}(N)_{\underline a}
-(u)_{\underline a}(N)_{\underline b}.                         \tag{31}
\]
To prove it, first suppose \(b=a+d\). Factoring the first \(a\) terms gives
\[
(u)_{\underline a}(N)_{\underline a}
\left((u-a)_{\underline d}-(N-a)_{\underline d}\right).       \tag{32}
\]
Because \(a\ge1\), \(u\mid(u)_{\underline a}\) and
\(N\mid(N)_{\underline a}\), giving two factors of \(q\). For every polynomial \(F\in\mathbb Z[X]\), \(U-V\mid F(U)-F(V)\). Applying this to \(F(X)=(X)_{\underline d}\), with \(U=u-a\), \(V=N-a\), shows that the bracket in (32) is divisible by \(u-N\), giving the third factor of \(q\). If instead \(a>b\), interchange \(a,b\); the expression changes only by a sign. This proves (31).

Now assume
\[
q=p^{k-1}\mid N,
\qquad x=sN.
\]
Put \(u=x-N=(s-1)N\). Then
\[
q\mid N,
\qquad q\mid u,
\qquad q\mid u-N=(s-2)N.                                      \tag{33}
\]
For \(j\ge3\) and \(1\le L\le j-1\), (28), (31), and (33) imply that
\[
q^3\mid j!Y,                                                    \tag{34}
\]
where
\[
Y=\binom xj\bigl(\mathcal C(x-j,N-L)
                 -\mathcal C(x-j,N-(j-L))\bigr).               \tag{35}
\]

We claim that (34) upgrades to
\[
p^{3k}\mid p^jY.                                               \tag{36}
\]
Let \(v=v_p(j!)\), and write \(j!=p^vw\), where \(p\nmid w\). The standard factorial valuation estimate
\[
(p-1)v_p(j!)<j
\]
follows, for instance, from Legendre’s formula
\(v_p(j!)=\sum_{r\ge1}\lfloor j/p^r\rfloor\). Since \(p-1\ge4\) and \(j\ge3\), this implies
\[
v\le j-3.                                                       \tag{37}
\]
From (34), multiplication by \(p^j\) shows that \(p^j j!Y\) is divisible by
\[
p^{j+3(k-1)}.
\]
By (37), \(j+3(k-1)\ge3k+v\). Hence
\[
p^{3k+v}\mid p^j j!Y=p^{j+v}wY.
\]
Cancel \(p^v\), and then cancel \(w\), which is coprime to \(p^{3k}\). This proves (36).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Pairing by antisymmetry
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix an outer index \(i\) in (27), put
\[
j=i+1,
\qquad x=sN,
\]
and denote the inner sum by
\[
S_i=\sum_{l=0}^{N}\pi_i(N-l)\binom{x-j}{l}.
\]
After the change of variable \(L=N-l\), this is
\[
S_i=\sum_{L=0}^{N}\pi_i(L)\mathcal C(x-j,N-L).                 \tag{38}
\]
We may extend the range to \(0\le L\le j\). Terms with \(L>N\) vanish because the lower index \(N-L\) is negative, while terms with \(L\ge j=i+1\) vanish by (21). Thus
\[
S_i=\sum_{L=0}^{j}\pi_i(L)\mathcal C(x-j,N-L).                 \tag{39}
\]
Reflect the index \(L\mapsto j-L\) in a second copy of this sum and use (19). We obtain
\[
2S_i=\sum_{L=0}^{j}\pi_i(L)
\left(\mathcal C(x-j,N-L)-\mathcal C(x-j,N-(j-L))\right).      \tag{40}
\]

Multiply (40) by \(p^j\binom xj\). We show term by term that the resulting right-hand side is divisible by \(p^{3k}\).

For \(L=0\), the coefficient \(\pi_i(0)\) is zero by (20). For \(L=j\), it is zero by (21). Thus only
\(1\le L\le j-1\) matters.

If \(j=1\), there are no interior values of \(L\). If \(j=2\), the only interior value is \(L=1\), and the two generalized binomial terms in parentheses in (40) are identical, so their difference is zero. Finally, if \(j\ge3\), divisibility by \(p^{3k}\) is exactly (36); multiplication by the extra integer \(\pi_i(L)\) does not affect it. Therefore
\[
p^{3k}\mid 2p^j\binom xjS_i.                                  \tag{41}
\]
Since \(p\ge5\) is odd, \(2\) is coprime to \(p^{3k}\), and it can be cancelled from (41). Hence
\[
p^{3k}\mid p^j\binom xjS_i.                                  \tag{42}
\]
This is precisely the divisibility of the \(i\)-th outer summand in (27), with \(M=x=sN\).

Summing (42) over \(0\le i<pN\) in (27) proves
\[
p^{3k}\mid [X^{pN}]B_{spN}\Phi-[X^N]B_{sN}\Phi,
\]
which is the coefficient theorem (7).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(n,k\) be positive integers and put
\[
N=np^{k-1}.
\]
Then \(N>0\), \(p^{k-1}\mid N\), and \(np^k=pN\). Apply (7) with
\[
s=m+2.
\]
Using (5), we obtain
\[
A_m(np^k)-A_m(np^{k-1})
=[X^{pN}]B_{(m+2)pN}\Phi-[X^N]B_{(m+2)N}\Phi
\equiv0\pmod{p^{3k}}.
\]
If one uses the quotient-normalized generalized sequence, formula (6) adds the same constant \(\mathbf1_{m=-1}\) to both sides, so the identical congruence follows there as well.

Taking \(m=4\), \(A_4(N)\) is exactly the value at \(1\) of the degree-\(N\) Taylor truncation of \(c(x)^{4N}\), namely A333096. Therefore, for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers \(n,k\),
\[
\boxed{\ a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod{p^{3k}}\ }.
\]
